utterances.text: I'm not in Negoslavci at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who could this possibly have been. Well, we have to go back to the theoretical aspect of the situation. The theory says it could have been the commander. But at this particular point in time, someone could have gone over there. I'm talking about the purely practical aspect. It could have been the soldier on duty outside the command who could have gone there and said that the unit was to go and they were right there. So I'm telling you about what happens in practice. There is a guard on the security job. He could have gone on, and this would have been complied with, and there would have been nothing wrong with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this is the way the order was executed.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, nobody would have asked questions about it. If that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the question. The witness has already answered it now twice that he is not the compiler of the document, he is not able to say who compiled the document, who the person is, and Mr. Lukic hasn't got the answer because the witness can't help and he's just pursuing point which is impossible for the witness to answer. He's being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, have you any submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll just move on. We'll soon have another witness who will probably be better-placed to talk about this. I just wanted to refresh the witness's memory but that was that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the simple answer is, I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked with Trifunovic; obviously he jogged your memory about those days. What about now? Do you remember seeing Vojnovic at the brigade command before you left for Ovcara? You said you were with your unit and you may have passed by the command and paid him a call. My specific question is: Did you see Vojnovic at the brigade command then as you were headed for Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've said this. I don't remember. I probably paid them a call, I did see people there, but whether Lieutenant-Colonel was there or not is really not something that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about Trifunovic and Sapic? Were they often with the commander's security in those days? Rather than often, were they with those soldiers at all, the soldiers who were providing security for the commander over the previous days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I don't remember, but I'll give it my best shot. They were both young lads, strong. One of them was even a karate expert. Whenever I could, you do have to bear in mind that this is a very delicate task, providing security for a commander that's on the move. I would send them on those assignments. How many times, I don't know. I don't know how many times the commander left. Whenever he was off somewhere, somebody would always be there escorting him, protecting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Trifunovic ever tell you that he had seen Vojnovic at the command and that he had looked distinctly unsettled? Is it possible for Trifunovic to actually see the commander and for you just simply not to notice him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to give an answer a while ago, and I'll try to do the same thing now. I don't like to talk about those events, but it was by pure coincidence as we were waiting inside the court building that we talked about a number of things. Then he reminded me of a couple of details to do with our trip then and the time when these things happened, but I don't remember him telling me anything else about that. And at the time I don't remember him telling me anything because it was very difficult to talk in the vehicle itself. I was sitting next to the driver on the passenger's seat and he was at the back. He was in the back of the car in the back seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll just skip my next question. Can we now please look at 256, that is the set, and the photograph number is 24. It's Exhibit 256. The set is 256, the photograph is 24. That's the one. A simple question. Does this photograph ring a bell, Mr. Vezmarovic? This photograph was taken later on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be the hangar inside which the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The prisoners too, presumably, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We can see the entrance to the right and the general direction of this photograph is towards the yellow house, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please try to indicate on this photograph where you set up the rope. I'm talking about the 20th now. Can you use this photograph, or perhaps you would like to use a different one to describe where you set up that rope to rope the prisoners off, as it were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I could try to use this one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: One at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right you can see the entrance. The right-hand side of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please mark that as number 1.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the entrance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the entrance, the prisoners were to the right of the entrance. So you go in, and the prisoners were to the right. The rope, well, I'll try to mark the rope as being here down the middle, but it was actually lower down in terms of height. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the prisoners were at the far end of the hangar looking from our current perspective, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were the one who set up the rope, the rope was not there before you got there, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek that this be admitted into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have photograph 23, please, from the same set of photographs. 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help me. Was this one taken from a different angle? If you don't know, then we have no use for this photograph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the same angle, then I would say it's the other way around. This is the opposite angle. This is the other door where the machines were, right? Yes. The machines were to the right. That's where I wanted to keep those soldiers as reserve, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this was from -- taken from where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the -- there were sliding doors at both ends of the hangar, but only one was used, and you must have fastened the one remaining door to keep it from being opened by someone else, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent that I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this door opens on to that yard across the way from those farming machines, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No need to mark this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender it as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it an exhibit already? I'm told it is, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's part of this 256 collection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Then no need to tender this, since the witness made no markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You arrive on the 20th, it is dark, so to speak. Right. You have just arrived, you realise that some of your soldiers from the military police company are there already, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see a number of soldiers from other units that were part of your brigade. Also you see a number of officers there, one of which you recognise, Joca Kafic. His real name was Jovan Novkovic, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Witness nods]. I'm trying not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was one of his soldiers that was drawing up a list, that's what you remember, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The previous answer on page 49, line 25, was yes. You were looking around to see if you could find anyone there who looked like a commander, a superior officer so that you could talk to him about establishing order or something, right? I'm not saying an officer, but someone in addition to Novkovic, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't looking around. I was asking. I spoke up to ask if there was anyone there who was in command of those units. Or, rather, I was asking for the most senior officer present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I suppose were you also sort of looking around the hangar to see if you could find anyone there to seemed to be highly ranked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking and specifically asking by using my voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you were looking around. You were searching. Do you remember seeing Vojnovic or Dragi Vukosavljevic there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session for a brief moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate -- is there a problem, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the transcript, which is convenient for me to follow in order to avoid overlaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You gave an order for everybody to leave. Everybody left with the exception of your military policemen guarding the hangar. Some complained and some didn't, but everybody left, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be easier for us to start overlapping now since I don't have the transcript in front of me. I have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This captain first class Novkovic was among those who left, right? Did you exchange any sort of information with him at this time? Specifically, did you ask him if there had been any trouble? I'll ask you what Borovic asked you yesterday. The moment you got there, did you ask Novkovic if anyone had beaten anyone else, if anyone had killed anyone else, if anyone had taken anybody else away? Did you ask him any questions at all, or did he just tell you unprompted, or did you simply not speak about this, or did you ask him and he said no, there was nothing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it in the simplest possible terms, I don't remember. When I arrived, my line of thinking and what I, in fact, did was to guard the prisoners to make sure they were safe. To make sure they were being guarded under my command. And then everything else would have followed. At this point in time, I did not stop to speak to anyone. I did not stop to arrange anything with anyone. I did not stop to take any decisions. I decided that everybody should leave because I had no idea where they belonged to, with the exception of the military policemen, the people with the white belts. The objective being to establish control over the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you were in the hangar with your military police officers, some of them having arrived earlier, this wasn't just for a fraction of a second, you did stay there for some time. Did any of your military police officers who had been there before tell you about any sort of mistreatment or people being taken away before you eventually arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think you probably would remember if anything like that had, in fact, been the case, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think so too, but it's just an assumption. It's pure speculation. Had anyone told me anything at the time, had there been any need to report, even the next day, to our commander, I certainly would have done so. But this is all in the realm of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you please take a look at your statement to the military court, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Judges for not providing copies of the statements, but I was surprised by something, and this is what I was to explain. I wasn't -- I didn't know whether you would want to have the entire statements or only the relevant portions to -- that are put to the witness. Perhaps we could get some instructions, and I believe I'm saying on behalf of my colleagues as well, asking for this instruction, to know whether you want to see the entire statement or just parts of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it is a statement, the entire statement. If it is a transcript of a full court hearing, the relevant part. By that I don't merely mean the question you're going to put and the answer, but what closely comes before and after so that the general context can be seen. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise again. This is new instruction compared to what we have been given before, and I also had some time to consult my clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... some of your colleagues have been doing this. Carry on, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe you have the statement you gave before the military court in front of you. Page 5. This is what you stated then, the second paragraph. "Upon my arrival at Ovcara I found the unit commanded by Joca. I asked him what has been going on at Ovcara in the meantime. He told me that the command had given him the task of guarding the prisoners in the hangar until the military police arrived." Do you remember having stated that before the military court and did you have such a conversation with Novkovic in 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that I don't remember, but back in 1999 we were much closer to the events of 1991 than we are now. And this is the first time I am being reminded after so long, and after all the statements I've given about having said this. So you keep jogging my memory, but it would have been far easier for me, had I been given these statements prior to the testimony to go through them and to have them before me even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any case, your recollection of events back in 1999 was far better than it is today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time your assessment was that with your 15 to 20 policemen you could set up security in the hangar in a proper way, that's why you wanted everyone to go out. Have I understood the situation correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from it being a sufficient number, but that's what I had at my disposal at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you needed more men at that moment, why did you order Novkovic and his men to leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have mentioned that before, but the simplest way to establish order and command was to have all the military policemen wearing white belts stay. In my assessment that was the best way to ensure security of the prisoners. Perhaps I can stop here and then your questions may follow. But this was my idea as to how to do it in the most efficient way. I couldn't discuss who was from what unit, and who wanted to stay and who was told what by whom. The people I didn't know had to leave, those I did could stay. And then we were supposed to decide what to do next.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then your instructions were obeyed to or complied with and when your military policemen remained, were there any problems as of that moment when you yourselves have been providing security?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't ask Novkovic to notify any of the officers from the command to send more policemen to assist or -- and you didn't ask for any other reinforcements from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know whether there were any additional policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And during the time you were there, before Karanfilov's arrival, you didn't send out any of your policemen to notify everyone that reinforcements were needed while you were inside, before Karanfilov arrived?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To go back to one of my previous answers, I'll just try to rephrase. I tried to provide proper security of the prisoners. As to how long it took, what the effort was, and everything that was going on, I can't remember. My primary task was to establish order. Once it has been, Captain Karanfilov came. Therefore, I had no time to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the last portion of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So during that time interval -- the end of the witness's answer has not been recorded on page 55, line 17. The end was "to be given another task to withdraw." That's what the witness said. As you were trying to gain control of the hangar, you didn't want or you didn't find it necessary to send anyone out to ask for reinforcements. That's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my assessment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Belgrade proceedings, page 82. I don't think I'll be putting it to the witness. Oh, yes, I will. I believe that is page 81 in the English. Attorney-at-law Milan Stanic, towards the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 82, line 15 from the bottom, more or less. Attorney-at-law Milan Stanic: "How many soldiers did he have at his disposal? What was the numerical strength?" Presiding judge: "He was asked that and he said 15 to 20 soldiers." Attorney-at-law Stanic: "In his estimate, would he have managed to continue securing -- to successfully secure these prisoners?" Witness Dragan Vezmarovic: "Yes. Absolutely. May I?" Presiding judge: "Yes, yes." Your reply; Witness Vezmarovic: "Everything could have been done in a regular way as regards security. Because everybody respected the newly established situation. Therefore, there were no problems." Do you remember having stated this, and do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was recorded this way, it means that I must have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on then. To be precise, I have another thing I wanted to clarify. During your stay in the hangar, the security was provided only by the military police of your brigade; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, while you were there, did other soldiers come to the hangar, or other officers, and I have in mind the JNA, and TO members as well. Did anyone enter the hangar while you were there apart from the moment when Karanfilov came, according to what you stated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all the details, but whether there were some other officers in front of the hangar, around the hangar, maybe they even went in, but I can't remember that. As regards the TO members who tried to enter, that was under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the way you described it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since security was provided, there was no problem with the soldiers of the 80th Motorised Brigade being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in the hangar, did any of the prisoners -- were any of the prisoners taken out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see a woman in the hangar who was one of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were pointing at a woman in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One woman? If you don't remember ...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were pointing at this particular woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've described the arrival of Karanfilov, he came, gave you instructions. In your estimate, how long did it take for him to issue the instructions before -- and for you to leave the hangar and Ovcara? Could you be somewhat specific?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try and do some math. We -- he came, we spoke, I was given an assignment, I issued orders, my soldiers assembled, the vehicles came, we packed our stuff. But I don't know how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said the vehicles arrived. What I thought was that the Pinzgauers were there, nearby. They didn't return to Negoslavci in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were there. They were parked and then brought closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And when Karanfilov told you the things he did, the situation in the hangar was fully under control; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe in your testimony here you stated that you were quite happy about not having to spend the night freezing there, and that the task was taken over by another unit, that is the TO to be specific.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may sound terrible, but it is true nonetheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it looks terrible from where you're sitting today, but at that moment could you have sensed or thought that something could take place? Did you think, well, I can go away for the night, but something might happen? Could you have anticipated that something would happen, something bad would happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no indications about anything bad happening. I had no doubt in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just before you got on the Pinzgauers, you had your policemen securing the inside of the hangar and just outside of the hangar, around the hangar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the military court, I won't read it out now, but I wanted to ask you this: The people to whom Karanfilov told them that they were to take over the duties there, being the TO officers, that you pointed it out to them that they were to behave in keeping the Geneva Conventions. That's what you stated in that -- before that tribunal, but do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having said that. What comes to mind is that I asked him whether they had sufficient numbers of men and whether they could provide adequate security, as far as I can could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 5 of that statement in the middle, third paragraph. You stated: "I couldn't see anything unusual. I couldn't have anticipated as to how they would treat them subsequently. I told the TO members to treat the prisoners fairly and according to the Geneva Conventions as regards those captured during combat operations. I thought that was the way they understood what I had said." Now that I've read this out, do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that before the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What surprises me is that you found it necessary to say all that to them, since Karanfilov was there. I don't know whether you remember that. Do you have any comment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm trying to explain the following: What was happening in the field was the way it was. And this fact that I may have addressed them, Karanfilov probably did too. We did that with the intention of meeting the goal that was set.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Two days before that you went through the handing over of the prisoners on the 18th, that is the 19th in the morning concerning the Mitnica group, and you have explained the procedure. Since you found nothing unusual about the TO units taking over the security of the prisoners, why didn't you ask for a list to be compiled first, the way you had asked two days before that? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember what I said about those two days, I didn't ask the list to be compiled by the people who took them prisoners. But rather, I compiled the list. So the people providing security were supposed to make a list. Therefore, logically, the TO was to make that list. If you understand what I'm trying to say. I wasn't the person who made --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, I made the list of the Mitnica prisoners who were handed over to me.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Therefore, to my logic the unit taking over was supposed to make the list. If I did that the previous night, then the group securing them should do that the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hand over the prisoners at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Much the same as the Mitnica group before. The principle was the same. The group was disgorged from the vehicles, they were sent inside. I didn't know how many there were. And the same applied to this time. They were all there. I saw them all, I left them, and my soldiers left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vezmarovic, I don't think you're answering my question, with all due respect, and it's basically a simple one. This moment when Karanfilov tells you that they would be taking charge, and then you leave, is this the hand-over of prisoners that you mean? Secondly, the unit now guarding the prisoners, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, in some way, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You did not believe at the time that first you should draw up a list of those persons before you handed them over to another unit, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VEZMAROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am about to wrap up. You talked about half past 12.00, but I have another 20 minutes to go, so I'm not sure if I should continue. Yesterday I understood that we would be continuing until 12.30 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our normal morning sessions on these mid-week days is 9.30 to 12.30, then 1.30 to 4.30. That's with why I said 12.30, to give you the complete afternoon. 20 minutes, I think, is a fairly substantial intrusion into that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think it would be preferable for everybody to keep to the time indicated, unless you see a significant problem there, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I was just wondering whether I should move on to my final topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, and we're always encouraged by the thought that whenever we give you an opportunity to think over a break, you are shorter after the break. So we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.30, as indicated. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of May, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.35 p.m.,
